title: Three Schema Architecture
description: Distinguish external, conceptual, and internal schemas through Payroll and HR views, explicit mappings, physical representation, and the practical limits of data independence.
notes:
## Separating three views of the same database

The three-schema architecture, commonly associated with the ANSI-SPARC model, distinguishes external, conceptual, and internal descriptions of a database. The external level concerns what particular users or applications work with. The conceptual level concerns the overall logical model within the database's scope. The internal level concerns physical representation and access. Separating these descriptions helps explain how interfaces can remain usable while other aspects of a system change.

The architecture expresses a design goal rather than a universal product implementation. It does not mean every DBMS has exactly three independent schema objects or that every change is automatically invisible to applications. Actual compatibility depends on the definitions, mappings, features, and callers in the system. Use the model to identify dependencies and intended boundaries instead of treating the three names as proof that those dependencies have disappeared.

The word schema also has product-specific uses. In SQL products it can name a namespace or a container for objects. That use is not identical to the three architectural viewpoints discussed here. A database can use SQL namespaces while still exposing tightly coupled application interfaces, and a useful architectural separation can involve views or application contracts rather than three objects literally named external, conceptual, and internal.

## Starting with a logical employee model

Consider a fictional database whose modeled Employee entity includes EmpID, Name, Salary, and DeptID. EmpID identifies an employee in this simplified example. The model must define what the other attributes mean and which rules apply to them. The conceptual description answers those logical questions without requiring a payroll caller to know the physical address or byte layout of an employee record.

The scope matters. Calling the conceptual schema the overall logical model means the coherent model for the database being described. It is not a requirement that every organization place all of its systems into one enormous model. Nor does it mean every application owns a separate unrelated conceptual truth about the same records. State the database and requirements being modeled when using the term.

A conceptual description also includes relevant relationships and constraints, not merely a list of field names. If a department reference is mandatory or employee identifiers must be unique, those rules are part of what the model needs to explain. A physical index may help enforce or access some representation, but its byte arrangement is a different kind of information from the meaning of the employee relationship.

## Defining external views for actual tasks

Suppose Payroll needs EmpID, Name, and Salary, while HR needs EmpID, Name, and DeptID. These are two external views of the same underlying employee model. They let each caller work with the information appropriate to its task without making every caller depend on every conceptual attribute. The views need not imply separate physical copies of all the employee records.

An external view can do more than select a literal subset of columns. It can rename values, combine information, or present a derived value where that is the intended interface. Finance might call the same conceptual salary attribute Pay. The mapping must establish which logical fact that label represents. Different names should not accidentally create two competing definitions of the same measurement.

An external view also does not itself prove an authorization policy. Restricting an interface to particular fields can support a useful contract, but trusted access mechanisms must enforce the actual permitted operations and records. A caller who can bypass an interface may still have other capabilities unless the system constrains them appropriately. Architectural separation and least-privilege enforcement are related design concerns, not interchangeable guarantees.

## Describing physical representation separately

The internal description concerns how the system represents and accesses data. Pages, record formats, indexes, file organization, and related access structures belong to this viewpoint. For example, a purely hypothetical internal design might use fixed-width sixty-four-byte employee records with a B-plus-tree access structure. That statement describes a chosen teaching example, not a claim about MySQL's or every DBMS's default record format.

Applications normally should not calculate record addresses from that detail. If the operator changes an index or the engine reorganizes physical storage, a suitable logical interface can continue to describe employees by EmpID and their attributes. This is the purpose of separating logical meaning from physical access. The actual product and change still need appropriate verification; a diagram is not permission to perform an operational modification.

Internal changes can have important effects even when the logical result is compatible. An index can affect performance and maintenance costs. A physical reorganization can have operational requirements. Saying that an external interface need not change does not mean the change has no consequences at all. Keep logical compatibility separate from claims about latency, availability, or the authorization to carry out maintenance.

## Connecting the levels through mappings

External-to-conceptual mappings explain how a caller's view corresponds to the overall logical model. They connect Payroll's Salary and Finance's Pay to the intended conceptual attribute. They can also describe a derived value. If Salary is explicitly defined as monthly base pay under a twelve-equal-period example, an AnnualSalary value can be defined as Salary multiplied by twelve. Different compensation rules would need a different definition rather than an assumed universal formula.

The conceptual-to-internal mapping connects logical objects and operations to their physical representation. A logical employee lookup need not expose which page or index access supplies it. The architecture distinguishes that dependency from the external mapping, which concerns the user's logical interface. Implementations can distribute the concrete work across database definitions and application facilities; the mapping names are conceptual responsibilities rather than a required pair of standalone programs.

Mappings must remain correct as definitions evolve. If a conceptual attribute changes meaning but an external label and calculation remain unchanged, a caller may receive plausible-looking values with the wrong interpretation. Successful query execution does not establish that the mapping still expresses the intended measurement. Compatibility requires checking meanings and constraints as well as names and types.

## Understanding physical and logical independence

Physical data independence concerns changing internal representation without forcing corresponding changes in the conceptual or external interfaces. Adding a suitable index is a common illustration. Payroll can continue asking for the same logical attributes while the runtime obtains them through a different access path. This is a goal supported by abstraction, not a claim that every product permits every physical change without any operational planning.

Logical data independence concerns changing the conceptual model while preserving useful external contracts where feasible. A stable view or other interface can sometimes protect a caller when underlying relations are reorganized. This is often harder because the caller may depend on the very meaning, shape, or relationship being changed. An omitted or reinterpreted required attribute cannot always be hidden behind an unchanged label.

For example, adding an unrelated logical attribute may leave an explicit Payroll view intact. Removing Salary from the model without providing a compatible way to supply its meaning would affect that view. The architecture helps reveal the dependency; it does not invent the missing information. A correct explanation of independence acknowledges which contracts can actually be maintained and which changes require caller coordination.

## Reviewing a proposed change using the model

Identify the level of the proposed change first. Is it a new reporting name, a revised relationship rule, or a different physical access structure? Then identify the mappings and callers that depend on it. Check whether the intended external results, meanings, and access boundaries remain correct. A developer's reliance on every current table column can create coupling even if the architecture drawing shows three clean layers.

Use concrete examples to verify the account. Payroll and HR should still receive their intended employee attributes after a compatible index change. A renamed external label should still map to the same defined conceptual fact. A new annual calculation should state its units and assumptions. These checks make the architecture useful without promising that a set of labels automatically provides compatibility, security, or performance.

The model is therefore a way to reason about responsibilities and change. External views describe task-facing information, the conceptual schema describes the coherent logical model, and the internal schema describes physical representation. Correct mappings connect them. Keep those distinctions and their practical limits clear, and the architecture becomes a tool for examining real dependencies rather than a diagram to memorize without understanding.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of the Three Schema (ANSI-SPARC) Architecture?
options: To separate user views, the logical database design, and physical storage so changes at one level do not force changes at the others
To speed up disk I/O by compressing tables
To enforce that every application must use the same SQL dialect
To replace the need for a conceptual schema entirely
questions.explanation: Separating viewpoints and mappings supports data-independence goals where compatible contracts can be preserved. It does not make every possible change automatically invisible.

questions.question_text: In the college database example, which level defines that `Employee` is stored as fixed-width 64-byte rows indexed by a B+-tree?
options: External schema
Conceptual schema
Internal schema
Middleware layer
questions.explanation: Physical storage details like record layout and indexing structure belong to the internal schema.

questions.question_text: What connects the three levels of the architecture and allows one level to change without breaking another?
options: The external/conceptual and conceptual/internal mappings
A shared connection pool
A single unified SQL driver
The database's transaction log
questions.explanation: The two mappings between adjacent levels are what enable logical and physical data independence.

questions.question_text: The Payroll app sees `(EmpID, Name, Salary)` and the HR app sees `(EmpID, Name, DeptID)` from the same underlying `Employee` table. What does this illustrate?
options: Two different external schemas built over one conceptual schema
Two different conceptual schemas over one internal schema
Two internal schemas sharing one external schema
A database middleware translation layer
questions.explanation: Multiple external schemas can each expose a tailored subset of the same single conceptual schema.

questions.question_text: If Payroll names a field `Salary` and Finance names the same conceptual attribute `Pay`, at what point must this naming conflict be resolved?
options: In the internal schema's storage layout
In each external schema's own mapping to the conceptual schema
It cannot be resolved without merging both applications
By renaming the conceptual attribute itself to match both
questions.explanation: Each external schema has its own external/conceptual mapping, so naming differences are resolved per view without altering the shared conceptual schema.

questions.question_text: A DBA re-indexes the `Employee` table for faster lookups. Under a correctly implemented three-schema architecture, what should happen to the Payroll and HR external schemas?
options: Both must be rewritten to reference the new index
Nothing — they remain unaffected since indexing is an internal-level change
Only the conceptual schema needs to change, not external schemas
The mappings must be deleted and rebuilt from scratch
questions.explanation: Re-indexing is purely an internal-schema change; a correctly designed architecture shields external schemas from it entirely.

questions.question_text: An external schema exposes a virtual column `AnnualSalary = Salary * 12`. Where must the logic to compute this value live?
options: Physically stored as an extra column in the internal schema
In the external/conceptual mapping, since `AnnualSalary` is derived, not stored
It cannot be exposed through an external schema at all
In the internal schema's index definition
questions.explanation: Computed/derived columns exposed to users are handled by the mapping between the external and conceptual levels, not stored physically.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes the conceptual schema from an external schema in this architecture?
options: The conceptual schema describes the overall logical model in scope; an external schema presents task-facing information that can restrict, rename or derive values
Every external view must include every conceptual attribute
The conceptual schema is only a physical file address
An external schema automatically grants all administrative privileges
questions.explanation: External views are task-specific logical representations, not necessarily literal subsets of stored columns. Their mappings must define the intended meaning.

questions.question_text: Does an SQL schema namespace automatically establish all three architectural levels?
options: Yes; every namespace creates every independence guarantee
No; product namespace terminology and architectural viewpoints are different concepts
Yes; callers can no longer depend on table definitions
No; architectural models can never use database views
questions.explanation: The architecture describes responsibilities and dependencies. A namespace is a particular product-level organizational facility.

questions.question_text: Can an external view rename or derive values instead of only selecting literal stored columns?
options: No; all views must reproduce every stored byte
Yes; derived values require no measurement definition
No; every user must see every conceptual attribute
Yes; the mapping must define the intended relationship to the conceptual facts
questions.explanation: An external interface can present a task-specific representation, but the definition and meaning of its values must be explicit.

questions.question_text: Payroll uses EmpID, Name and Salary while HR uses EmpID, Name and DeptID. What is illustrated?
options: Two necessarily separate physical copies of every employee
A universal requirement for identical views
Different external views over one scoped conceptual employee model
Proof that every account has the right privileges
questions.explanation: The callers need different task-facing information while referring to the same modeled employee facts.

questions.question_text: An illustrative design specifies sixty-four-byte employee records and a B-plus-tree. Which viewpoint does that detail describe?
options: Internal physical representation and access
Only the Payroll display label
The complete authorization policy
An automatically enforced organization-wide rule
questions.explanation: Record layout and access structures concern the internal description, not the caller's logical task interface.

questions.question_text: Finance calls a conceptual salary value Pay. What needs an explicit mapping?
options: The label to an arbitrary unrelated field
The external label to the intended conceptual attribute and meaning
Every employee to a new physical person
Only the font size used in the report
questions.explanation: Different external names must still refer to the intended logical fact.

questions.question_text: AnnualSalary is defined as Salary times twelve. What assumption needs to be stated in this illustration?
options: Every compensation arrangement everywhere is identical
Salary can mean any unit without affecting the result
Salary represents monthly base pay under the twelve-equal-period rule
The expression automatically verifies every business policy
questions.explanation: A calculation is meaningful only with the relevant measurement and policy assumptions.

questions.question_text: A suitable index is added while an explicit Payroll view remains compatible. Which independence goal does this illustrate?
options: Automatic permission to perform maintenance
Physical data independence
A guarantee of zero operational impact
A change from one employee identity to another
questions.explanation: The internal access path can change without changing the required logical interface, subject to actual product and compatibility checks.

questions.question_text: The conceptual Salary attribute is removed without any compatible replacement. What can the architecture alone not do?
options: Reveal that Payroll depends on that fact
Distinguish the conceptual change from a physical index change
Help identify the affected mapping
Supply the missing fact required by Payroll automatically
questions.explanation: A diagram exposes dependencies but cannot invent unavailable information to preserve an incompatible contract.

questions.question_text: A stable view shields a caller while underlying logical relations are reorganized. Which goal is being considered?
options: Logical data independence where the required contract can be preserved
A guarantee that all schema changes are always invisible
Proof that physical file addresses never change
A rule that every application owns a different truth
questions.explanation: Logical reorganization can sometimes be hidden through a compatible interface, but meanings and required values must remain supportable.

questions.question_text: The external screen hides Salary, but its account can query it through another unrestricted path. What remains unproven?
options: The actual authorization boundary for that attribute
Whether a screen can omit a field
Whether different views can exist
Whether the conceptual model has attributes
questions.explanation: An architectural view is not itself proof that every bypass path is constrained.

questions.question_text: An index change preserves query results but affects latency and maintenance work. Is that inconsistent with physical independence?
options: Yes; independence guarantees identical performance forever
Yes; physical changes cannot have costs
No; compatibility therefore needs no verification
No; interface compatibility does not imply zero operational consequences
questions.explanation: Separate the logical contract from operational and performance effects.

questions.question_text: Which proposed-change review best uses the architecture?
options: Approve the change solely because three boxes were drawn
Identify the changed level, dependent mappings, caller meanings, and required checks
Assume every namespace prevents every compatibility problem
Ignore the applications using the database
questions.explanation: The model supports dependency reasoning and verification, not automatic success claims.
